apsp-subcubic/1703.01638.claim: The authors do not present a new algorithm for all-pairs shortest paths (APSP), but instead use the existing APSP conjecture to prove conditional lower bounds for sensitivity graph problems.
apsp-subcubic/1703.01638.evidence: We give more lower bounds under the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis and the All Pairs Shortest Paths Conjecture.
apsp-subcubic/1703.01638.caveat: The paper assumes the hardness of APSP as a standard hypothesis to establish lower bounds rather than attempting to resolve the conjecture.

apsp-subcubic/1710.07601.claim: The authors do not claim to make progress on the APSP problem itself, but instead use the standard APSP conjecture as a conditional hardness assumption to establish kernelization lower bounds for parameterized problems.
apsp-subcubic/1710.07601.evidence: We prove that a linear-time computable strict kernel of truly subcubic size for this problem violates the popular APSP-conjecture.
apsp-subcubic/1710.07601.caveat: The paper relies on the assumed hardness of APSP as an unproven hypothesis to derive parameterized lower bounds, rather than proving new upper or lower bounds for APSP itself.

apsp-subcubic/1905.02298.claim: The preprint does not address or make any claims about the All-Pairs Shortest Paths problem, focusing instead on algorithms for elastic-degenerate string matching.
apsp-subcubic/1905.02298.evidence: None: the abstract does not mention All-Pairs Shortest Paths or graph shortest path algorithms.

apsp-subcubic/1910.04911.claim: The authors derive a truly subcubic algorithm for Min-Plus matrix multiplication under significantly relaxed structural constraints, yielding subcubic APSP algorithms for a broader class of geometric graphs.
apsp-subcubic/1910.04911.evidence: This result presents the most general case to date of Min-Plus product that is solvable in truly subcubic time.
apsp-subcubic/1910.04911.caveat: The subcubic Min-Plus product and APSP algorithms rely on specific structural conditions (matrices close to constant rank blocks or geometric graph properties) rather than general arbitrary edge weights.

apsp-subcubic/2105.02428.claim: The authors do not claim progress on all-pairs shortest paths itself, but rather present an $O(nk^2 \log n)$-time algorithm for bounded unweighted tree edit distance.
apsp-subcubic/2105.02428.evidence: In this paper, we give a faster algorithm taking $O(nk^2 \log n)$ time, improving both of the previous results for almost the full range of $\log n \ll k\ll n/\sqrt{\log n}$.
apsp-subcubic/2105.02428.caveat: The paper cites the APSP conjecture solely as fine-grained hardness motivation for weighted tree edit distance and does not address the APSP problem directly.

apsp-subcubic/2110.08782.claim: The authors present an improved randomized algorithm running in $O(n^{2.779})$ time for the min-plus product of $n\times n$ $\delta$-bounded-difference matrices with $\delta = O(1)$.
apsp-subcubic/2110.08782.evidence: In this paper, we focus on the min-plus product on a special class of matrices, called $\delta$-bounded-difference matrices, in which the difference between any two adjacent entries is bounded by $\delta=O(1)$. Our algorithm runs in randomized time $O(n^{2.779})$ by the fast rectangular matrix multiplication algorithm [Le Gall & Urrutia 18], better than $\tilde{O}(n^{2+w/3})=O(n^{2.791})$ ($w<2.373$ [Alman & V.V.Williams 20]).
apsp-subcubic/2110.08782.caveat: The algorithm applies only to the restricted class of $\delta$-bounded-difference matrices where $\delta=O(1)$, and does not yield a truly subcubic algorithm for general real-weighted APSP.

apsp-subcubic/2311.09095.claim: The abstract does not make a claim about all-pairs shortest paths, focusing instead on obtaining a faster combinatorial algorithm for Boolean Matrix Multiplication.
apsp-subcubic/2311.09095.evidence: We design a combinatorial algorithm for BMM running in time $n^3 / 2^{\Omega(\sqrt[7]{\log n})}$ -- a speed-up over cubic time that is stronger than any poly-log factor.
apsp-subcubic/2311.09095.caveat: The result is for combinatorial Boolean Matrix Multiplication rather than All-Pairs Shortest Paths on real-weighted graphs.

apsp-subcubic/2411.06502.claim: The authors establish a fine-grained equivalence between Tree Edit Distance (TED) and All-Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP), applying existing APSP bounds to TED without improving the running time for general APSP itself.
apsp-subcubic/2411.06502.evidence: Not only we show that TED is fine-grained equivalent to APSP, our reduction is tight enough, so that combined with the fastest APSP algorithm to-date [Williams 2018] it gives the first ever subcubic time algorithm for TED running in $n^3/2^{\frac{1}{2}\times\text{something}}$ time.
apsp-subcubic/2411.06502.caveat: The result uses established APSP algorithms to solve Tree Edit Distance, but does not provide a faster algorithm for general APSP or resolve the subcubic APSP conjecture.

cake-cutting-poly/2511.09882.claim: The authors claim to construct a private, envy-free, and strategyproof cake-cutting protocol using cryptographic techniques, without addressing query complexity bounds in the Robertson–Webb model.
cake-cutting-poly/2511.09882.evidence: To the best of our knowledge, we present the first private cake-cutting protocol, and, in addition, this protocol is also envy-free and strategyproof.
cake-cutting-poly/2511.09882.caveat: The work focuses on privacy constraints and cryptographic multi-party computation rather than query complexity bounds for general valuation functions in the Robertson–Webb model.

circuit-lower-bounds/1811.02725.claim: The authors show that proving certain polynomial cell-probe lower bounds for static data structures would conditionally imply superlinear circuit lower bounds for log-depth linear circuits.
circuit-lower-bounds/1811.02725.evidence: Our results further assert that polynomial ($t\geq n^\delta$) data structure lower bounds against near-optimal space, would imply super-linear circuit lower bounds for log-depth linear circuits (a four-decade open question).
circuit-lower-bounds/1811.02725.caveat: The result is conditional on unproven data structure lower bounds and targets log-depth linear circuits rather than general $O(n)$-size Boolean circuits over the full binary basis.

circuit-lower-bounds/1811.04828.claim: The authors propose structural depth-$3$ reductions for general Boolean circuits and show that improving certain pseudorandom constructions would yield new circuit size lower bounds, without directly proving an unconditional superlinear lower bound.
circuit-lower-bounds/1811.04828.evidence: While these structural results do not immediately lead to new lower bounds, they do suggest new avenues of attack on these longstanding lower bound problems.
circuit-lower-bounds/1811.04828.caveat: The paper presents structural depth-reduction techniques and conditional implications rather than an explicit unconditional lower bound exceeding $3n$ for a function in $\mathrm{NP}$.

circuit-lower-bounds/1902.07334.claim: The authors show that Fourier, circulant, and Toeplitz matrices are not rigid, thereby ruling out these matrix families as candidates for proving circuit lower bounds via Valiant's approach.
circuit-lower-bounds/1902.07334.evidence: In particular, we get that complex valued Fourier matrices, circulant matrices, and Toeplitz matrices are all not rigid and cannot be used to carry out Valiant's approach to proving circuit lower bounds.
circuit-lower-bounds/1902.07334.caveat: The paper presents a barrier/negative result for a specific technique (matrix rigidity) rather than proving a lower bound for functions in $\mathrm{NP}$.

circuit-lower-bounds/1910.11921.claim: The authors establish an equivalence between matrix rigidity and lower bounds for systematic linear data structures, proving new lower bounds for the vector-matrix-vector problem, but do not claim any superlinear Boolean circuit lower bounds for functions in $\mathrm{NP}$.
circuit-lower-bounds/1910.11921.evidence: In this work, we derive an equivalence between rigidity and the systematic linear model of data structures.
circuit-lower-bounds/1910.11921.caveat: The paper focuses on data structure lower bounds (in the systematic linear and cell probe models) and matrix rigidity rather than general Boolean circuit size lower bounds.

circuit-lower-bounds/2102.11992.claim: The author proves upper bounds on the circuit size of specific linear transformations and establishes non-rigidity results showing that certain matrix families cannot be used to prove linear-depth circuit lower bounds via Valiant's approach.
circuit-lower-bounds/2102.11992.evidence: A new rigidity upper bound, showing that the following classes of matrices are not rigid enough to prove circuit lower bounds using Valiant's approach: $-$ for any field $\mathbb{F}$ and any function $f : \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{F}$, the matrix $V_f \in \mathbb{F}^{2^n \times 2^n}$ given by, for any $x,y \in \{0,1\}^n$, $V_f[x,y] = f(x \wedge y)$, and $-$ for any field $\mathbb{F}$ and any fixed-size matrices $M_1, \ldots, M_n \in \mathbb{F}^{q \times q}$, the Kronecker product $M_1 \otimes M_2 \otimes \cdots \otimes M_n$.
circuit-lower-bounds/2102.11992.caveat: The preprint proves upper bounds and barrier results (non-rigidity) against Valiant's program, rather than proving superlinear Boolean circuit lower bounds for a function in $\mathrm{NP}$.

circuit-lower-bounds/2103.05631.claim: The author proves improved upper bounds on the matrix rigidity of Kronecker products, demonstrating that a wider class of matrices fails to be Valiant-rigid.
circuit-lower-bounds/2103.05631.evidence: As an application of our results we significantly expand the class of Hadamard matrices that are known not to be Valiant-rigid; these now include the Kronecker products of Paley-Hadamard matrices and Hadamard matrices of bounded size.
circuit-lower-bounds/2103.05631.caveat: The paper proves upper bounds on matrix rigidity (showing certain explicit matrices cannot yield circuit lower bounds via Valiant's program), rather than proving circuit lower bounds for functions in $\mathrm{NP}$.

circuit-lower-bounds/2603.22795.claim: The authors prove an exponential quantum-classical separation for one-way Numbers-on-Forehead communication complexity, but do not claim any new circuit lower bounds for $\mathrm{NP}$.
circuit-lower-bounds/2603.22795.evidence: In this paper, we resolve this open problem by establishing the first exponential separation between quantum and randomized communication complexity in one-way NOF model.
circuit-lower-bounds/2603.22795.caveat: The paper resolves an open problem in quantum communication complexity rather than establishing circuit lower bounds for functions in $\mathrm{NP}$.

circuit-lower-bounds/2607.15848.claim: The authors prove improved superlinear size lower bounds for low-depth arithmetic circuits rather than general Boolean circuits for functions in $\mathrm{NP}$.
circuit-lower-bounds/2607.15848.evidence: We improve Raz's superlinear bound quadratically (with circuit size to input size ratio as the metric) below $o(\log n/\log\log n)$ depths.
circuit-lower-bounds/2607.15848.caveat: The results concern arithmetic circuit complexity rather than Boolean circuit size lower bounds over the full binary basis.

circuit-lower-bounds/2608.08760.claim: The authors do not construct explicit functions hard for $O(n)$-size circuits, but instead show that formal proof systems such as $\mathrm{PCR}_{\mathbb{F}_2}$ cannot efficiently prove circuit lower bounds.
circuit-lower-bounds/2608.08760.evidence: We show that PCR$_{F_2}$ does not admit short proofs of lower-bound statements against Boolean circuits, nor against weak models of algebraic circuits.
circuit-lower-bounds/2608.08760.caveat: The paper studies the proof complexity of circuit lower bound formulas (metamathematics/unprovability) rather than proving explicit superlinear circuit lower bounds.

deterministic-linear-mst/2603.22063.claim: The authors adapt Kruskal's algorithm for computing minimum spanning trees to operate directly on DAG-compressed graph representations rather than addressing the deterministic linear-time MST problem for standard graphs in the comparison model.
deterministic-linear-mst/2603.22063.evidence: We add another entry to the list of algorithms where this is possible, by showing that Kruskal's algorithm for computing minimum spanning trees can be adapted to work directly on DAG compressions.
deterministic-linear-mst/2603.22063.caveat: The algorithm operates on DAG-compressed graphs rather than standard graph representations, and does not claim linear-time bounds in the general uncompressed setting.

deterministic-linear-mst/2606.31907.claim: The authors do not claim any result regarding the time complexity of computing standard minimum spanning trees, focusing instead on approximation algorithms for degree-bounded Traveling Salesman Problems.
deterministic-linear-mst/2606.31907.evidence: This improvement relies on a new lemma that enables the use of a bounded-degree minimum spanning tree, rather than a bounded-degree Steiner tree, as a starting point for the algorithm.

dynamic-optimality/2501.17563.claim: The authors analyze linear programming relaxations for optimal static search trees on trees, disproving Golinsky's conjecture that a specific LP formulation always yields an optimal static search tree on a tree.
dynamic-optimality/2501.17563.evidence: We show that the conjecture is false and that Golinsky's LP does not always give an optimal solution.
dynamic-optimality/2501.17563.caveat: The preprint studies static search trees on general tree topologies rather than the dynamic optimality conjecture or the competitiveness of splay trees on dynamic BST access sequences.

dynamic-optimality/2510.19175.claim: The preprint focuses on succinct dynamic rank/select data structures and compressed treaps, making no claims regarding the dynamic optimality conjecture or the competitiveness of splay trees.
dynamic-optimality/2510.19175.evidence: None of the abstract sentences discuss splay trees, offline binary search trees, or the dynamic optimality conjecture.

dynamic-optimality/2606.28889.claim: The authors propose a concurrent splay-inspired binary search tree variant using depth thresholds and access counters, proving static optimality for its sequential read-only version.
dynamic-optimality/2606.28889.evidence: We prove static optimality for the corresponding sequential read-only tree and evaluate both rotation designs by implementing them on top of the concurrent AVL tree of Bronson et al.
dynamic-optimality/2606.28889.caveat: The paper focuses on practical concurrent data structure design and static optimality for a modified tree structure, rather than addressing dynamic optimality of standard splay trees.

efx-existence/2606.08872.claim: The authors claim to resolve the existence of EFX allocations for indivisible chores by showing that EFX allocations do not always exist for $n \geq 4$ agents with additive cost functions.
efx-existence/2606.08872.evidence: We show that, even for tri-valued additive cost functions, for every $n\geq 4$, there exists an instance with $n$ agents where no EFX allocation exists.
efx-existence/2606.08872.caveat: The result is for indivisible chores (additive cost functions) rather than indivisible goods (additive utility functions), so it does not settle the open problem for goods.

efx-existence/2606.18665.claim: The authors claim to prove the existence of EFX allocations for an arbitrary number of agents under multigraph valuations, a special case where each good is valued by at most two agents.
efx-existence/2606.18665.evidence: In this paper, we resolve this open problem by proving the existence of EFX allocations for multigraph instances under cancelable valuations, a strict superclass of additive valuation functions.
efx-existence/2606.18665.caveat: The result is restricted to multigraph valuations, where each good has positive value for at most two agents, rather than general additive valuations.

efx-existence/2608.10572.claim: The authors prove that complete EFX allocations do not always exist for indivisible chores when agents have binary XOS or binary supermodular cost functions.
efx-existence/2608.10572.evidence: In this paper, we provide two counterexamples based on the same 18-agent, 53-chore word gadget, with one cost profile for binary XOS costs and another for binary supermodular costs.
efx-existence/2608.10572.caveat: The paper studies indivisible chores with non-additive cost functions, whereas the open problem asks about indivisible goods with additive valuation functions.

erdos-hajnal/1508.00634.claim: The authors prove a weaker variant of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture—which requires excluding both $H$ and its complement $H^c$—for an infinite family of graphs $H$ defined as paths with a pendant edge at their third vertex.
erdos-hajnal/1508.00634.evidence: We show that the weaker conjecture holds if $H$ is any path with a pendant edge at its third vertex; thus we give a new infinite family of graphs for which the conjecture holds.
erdos-hajnal/1508.00634.caveat: The paper proves only a weaker variant of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture (requiring exclusion of both $H$ and its complement $H^c$ rather than $H$ alone) for a specific family of graphs.

erdos-hajnal/1809.00919.claim: , the authors prove that for every forest $H$, any graph $G$ excluding both $H$ and its complement $\overline{H}$ as induced subgraphs contains a clique or stable set of size at least $|G|^c$ for some constant $c > 0$.
erdos-hajnal/1809.00919.evidence: It follows that for every forest H there is c > 0 so that if G contains neither H nor its complement as an induced subgraph then there is a clique or stable set of cardinality at least |G|^c.
erdos-hajnal/1809.00919.caveat: The result is restricted to forests $H$ (and requires excluding both $H$ and its complement $\overline{H}$), rather than establishing the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture for all fixed graphs $H$.

erdos-hajnal/2110.00278.claim: The authors establish a near-polynomial upper bound of $\omega^{\log_2(\omega)}$ on the chromatic number of $P_5$-free graphs, substantially improving upon the previous exponential bound toward settling the smallest open case of the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture.
erdos-hajnal/2110.00278.evidence: We prove that a $P_5$-free graph with clique number $ω\ge 3$ has chromatic number at most $ω^{\log_2(ω)}$.
erdos-hajnal/2110.00278.caveat: The result proves a near-polynomial bound rather than a polynomial bound, which means it approaches but does not fully resolve the Erdős–Hajnal conjecture even for the specific case of $P_5$.

erdos-szekeres/1206.4001.claim: The authors introduce a new pigeonhole proof of the Erdős–Szekeres cups-vs-caps theorem and establish bounds for related hypergraph Ramsey numbers, but do not claim to improve the bounds for the Erdős–Szekeres conjecture itself.
erdos-szekeres/1206.4001.evidence: We give a new pigeonhole proof of the Erdős-Szekeres Theorem on cups-vs-caps, similar to Seidenberg's proof of the Erdos-Szekeres Lemma on increasing/decreasing subsequences.
erdos-szekeres/1206.4001.caveat: The abstract focuses on hypergraph Ramsey numbers and alternative proofs of classical foundational results rather than proving new bounds for the exact number of points guaranteeing a convex $n$-gon.

erdos-szekeres/1604.08657.claim: The author claims an upper bound of $2^{n+o(n)}$ for the Erdős–Szekeres problem, matching the main term in the exponent of the conjectured $2^{n-2}+1$ bound.
erdos-szekeres/1604.08657.evidence: In this paper, we nearly settle the Erdos-Szekeres conjecture by showing that $ES(n) =2^{n +o(n)}$.
erdos-szekeres/1604.08657.caveat: The result determines the exponent's leading term but leaves lower-order terms open, so it does not establish the exact value $2^{n-2}+1$.

erdos-szekeres/1701.03333.claim: The authors introduce an Erdős–Szekeres type obstruction for representing finite convex geometries using ellipses, but do not address the Erdős–Szekeres conjecture itself.
erdos-szekeres/1701.03333.evidence: We present an Erdos-Szekeres type obstruction, which answers a question of Czedli negatively, that is general convex geometries cannot be represented with ellipses in the plane.
erdos-szekeres/1701.03333.caveat: The result concerns representation theory of finite convex geometries rather than point configurations in general position guaranteeing convex $n$-gons.

graph-isomorphism/1001.0608.claim: The authors do not address graph isomorphism, but instead present a quantum algorithm for a restricted class of the group isomorphism problem.
graph-isomorphism/1001.0608.evidence: In this paper we present a quantum algorithm solving the same problem in time polynomial in the logarithm of the order of the input groups.
graph-isomorphism/1001.0608.caveat: The result pertains to group isomorphism for specific group extensions in a quantum black-box model, rather than classical polynomial-time algorithms for general graph isomorphism.

graph-isomorphism/1205.1183.claim: The authors study Graph Isomorphism in a trial-and-error model with hidden inputs, proving that no time-efficient algorithm exists for it in this specific model under standard hardness assumptions.
graph-isomorphism/1205.1183.evidence: In particular, no time-efficient algorithms exist (under standard hardness assumptions) for Graph Isomorphism and Group Isomorphism problems.
graph-isomorphism/1205.1183.caveat: The hardness result holds in a non-standard trial-and-error oracle model with unknown inputs, rather than the standard computational model where the graphs are fully given.

graph-isomorphism/2303.15412.claim: The author presents an algorithm for group isomorphism on $p$-groups of class 2 and exponent $p$ running in $n^{O((\text{log } n)^{5/6})}$ time, which targets Group Isomorphism rather than Graph Isomorphism.
graph-isomorphism/2303.15412.evidence: In this paper, we present an isomorphism testing algorithm for $p$-groups of class 2 and exponent $p$ with running time $n^{O((\log n)^{5/6})}$ for any prime $p > 2$.
graph-isomorphism/2303.15412.caveat: The paper solves a case of the Group Isomorphism problem (for groups given by Cayley tables), which is a distinct problem from Graph Isomorphism.

graph-isomorphism/2410.06095.claim: The authors present polynomial-time canonical labelling algorithms for random graphs $G(n,p)$ across all edge probabilities $p$ and for arbitrary graphs subjected to small random edge perturbations.
graph-isomorphism/2410.06095.evidence: First, we consider randomly perturbed graphs, in accordance with the smoothed analysis philosophy of Spielman and Teng: for any graph $G$, naïve refinement becomes effective after a tiny random perturbation to $G$ (specifically, the addition and removal of $O(n\log n)$ random edges).
graph-isomorphism/2410.06095.caveat: The results apply to smoothed analysis and average-case analysis on random graphs, rather than providing a worst-case polynomial-time algorithm for Graph Isomorphism on arbitrary graphs.

graph-isomorphism/2412.07106.claim: The authors study the generalization abilities of message-passing graph neural networks using graph similarity theory and techniques connected to graph isomorphism testing, without claiming any new algorithm or complexity result for graph isomorphism itself.
graph-isomorphism/2412.07106.evidence: The expressive power of message-passing graph neural networks (MPNNs) is reasonably well understood, primarily through combinatorial techniques from graph isomorphism testing.
graph-isomorphism/2412.07106.caveat: The paper focuses on machine learning generalization bounds for graph neural networks rather than the computational complexity of the graph isomorphism problem.

graph-isomorphism/2504.19777.claim: The authors show that isomorphism testing for Fitting-free groups specified by a generating set of permutations is $\textsf{GI}$-hard, but they do not improve the complexity bounds for Graph Isomorphism itself.
graph-isomorphism/2504.19777.evidence: In sharp contrast, we show that when our groups are specified by a generating set of permutations, isomorphism testing of Fitting-free groups is at least as hard as Graph Isomorphism and Linear Code Equivalence (the latter being $\textsf{GI}$-hard and having no known subexponential-time algorithm).
graph-isomorphism/2504.19777.caveat: The paper uses Graph Isomorphism as a complexity class benchmark to classify group isomorphism variants rather than presenting new algorithms or bounds for Graph Isomorphism.

graph-isomorphism/2601.05892.claim: The authors analyze the power and limitations of the $k$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm for graph isomorphism on specific classes of graphs with small twin-width.
graph-isomorphism/2601.05892.evidence: We show that the graph isomorphism problem for graphs of twin-width 1 can be solved by the purely combinatorial 3-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm, while there is no fixed $k$ such that the $k$-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm solves the graph isomorphism problem for graphs of twin-width 4.
graph-isomorphism/2601.05892.caveat: The results are restricted to specific classes of small twin-width graphs and bounds on the Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm, rather than resolving graph isomorphism in general polynomial time.

graph-isomorphism/2604.13953.claim: The paper gives improved parallel algorithms for specific cases of Group Isomorphism, rather than general Graph Isomorphism.
graph-isomorphism/2604.13953.evidence: In this paper, we exhibit $\textsf{AC}^{3}$ isomorphism tests for coprime extensions $H \ltimes N$ where $H$ is elementary Abelian and $N$ is Abelian; and groups where $\text{Rad}(G) = Z(G)$ is elementary Abelian and $G = \text{Soc}^{*}(G)$.
graph-isomorphism/2604.13953.caveat: The paper addresses Group Isomorphism for restricted families of groups, not general Graph Isomorphism.

graph-isomorphism/2608.14486.claim: The authors present polynomial-time algorithms for testing isomorphism on restricted classes of tournaments, specifically those with bounded VC dimension or bounded chromatic number.
graph-isomorphism/2608.14486.evidence: Resolving an open problem of Neuen and Grohe, we show that the isomorphism problem for tournaments of VC dimension $d$ can be decided in time $n^{O(d\log d)}$.
graph-isomorphism/2608.14486.caveat: The algorithm applies only to specific classes of tournaments (bounded VC dimension and bounded chromatic number) rather than general tournaments or general graphs.

hadwiger/2002.11100.claim: The authors prove a lower bound on the size of a clique minor in $K_s$-free graphs as a function of independence number $\alpha(G)$ and vertex count $n$, addressing a variant problem inspired by Hadwiger's conjecture.
hadwiger/2002.11100.evidence: In particular, we show that any $K_s$-free graph has a clique minor of order $c_s(n/\alpha(G))^{1+\frac{1}{10(s-2)}}$, for some constant $c_s$ depending only on $s$.
hadwiger/2002.11100.caveat: The result applies to a restricted problem concerning $H$-free graphs and independence number rather than directly resolving or making major progress on Hadwiger's conjecture itself.

hadwiger/2203.02766.claim: The author proves a relaxation of Hadwiger's conjecture showing that every graph with no odd $K_t$-minor admits a vertex $(2t-2)$-coloring with monochromatic components of size at most $\lceil \frac{1}{2}(t-2) \rceil$.
hadwiger/2203.02766.evidence: We prove a relaxation of the above conjecture, namely we show that every graph with no odd $K_t$-minor admits a vertex $(2t-2)$-coloring such that all monochromatic components have size at most $\lceil \frac{1}{2}(t-2) \rceil$.
hadwiger/2203.02766.caveat: The result establishes an improper (clustered) coloring with bounded monochromatic component sizes rather than the proper graph coloring required by Hadwiger's conjecture.

hadwiger/2304.01823.claim: The authors establish a Robertson-Seymour type structure theorem for locally finite quasi-transitive graphs avoiding a minor and show such graphs attain their Hadwiger number, but do not address the colouring aspect of Hadwiger's conjecture.
hadwiger/2304.01823.evidence: Every locally finite quasi-transitive graph attains its Hadwiger number, that is, if such a graph contains arbitrarily large clique minors, then it contains an infinite clique minor.
hadwiger/2304.01823.caveat: The paper focuses on structural graph theory for infinite graphs and decidability of the domino problem, without addressing graph colouring or bounds on the chromatic number.

hadwiger-nelson/2304.10163.claim: The author proves that at least 7 colors are required to color the plane if the forbidden distance is expanded from $1$ to any interval $[1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon]$ for $\varepsilon > 0$.
hadwiger-nelson/2304.10163.evidence: The main result of the present paper is that the conjecture is true for the Euclidean plane as well as for any Minkowski plane.
hadwiger-nelson/2304.10163.caveat: The result addresses a variation where an interval of distances $[1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon]$ is forbidden, which yields a denser graph and does not improve the bounds for the single-distance Hadwiger--Nelson problem.

hadwiger-nelson/2501.18976.claim: The paper does not make any claim regarding the chromatic number of the plane, focusing instead on bootstrap percolation and $3$-cores in random lattice graphs.
hadwiger-nelson/2501.18976.evidence: We show that typically the size of the $3$-core of the corresponding induced unit-distance graph transitions from $0$ to $n-o(n)$ within a single step.

hadwiger-nelson/2606.28157.claim: The authors show that the fractional chromatic number of the plane is strictly greater than $4$, which concerns a related fractional variant of the problem but does not improve the known bounds $5 \le \chi \le 7$ on the ordinary chromatic number of the plane.
hadwiger-nelson/2606.28157.evidence: This disproves their Conjecture 1, and implies that the fractional chromatic number of the plane is strictly larger than 4.
hadwiger-nelson/2606.28157.caveat: The paper establishes a result on the fractional chromatic number and independence ratio, which does not improve the existing lower bound of $5$ for the chromatic number of the plane.

k-server/1905.07145.claim: The authors propose deterministic and randomized competitive online algorithms for an energy plan selection problem modeled as a variant of metrical task systems with temporally dependent switching costs.
k-server/1905.07145.evidence: We first formulate the online energy plan selection problem as a metrical task system problem with temporally dependent switching costs.
k-server/1905.07145.caveat: The paper focuses on a specific application-driven metrical task system model for energy plan selection rather than addressing the general $k$-server conjecture.

k-server/2003.02144.claim: The authors propose a prediction framework for metrical task systems (including $k$-server) to incorporate untrusted machine-learned predictions while guaranteeing robustness.
k-server/2003.02144.evidence: In this paper, we propose a prediction setup for arbitrary metrical task systems (MTS) (e.g., caching, k-server and convex body chasing) and online matching on the line.
k-server/2003.02144.caveat: The paper studies the learning-augmented online model with predictions rather than the standard worst-case competitive model of the deterministic $k$-server conjecture.

k-server/2111.10908.claim: The authors present an $O((\top)-...)$ / $O((\log n)^2)$-competitive algorithm for metrical task systems using multiscale entropic regularization directly on metric spaces, which shares techniques with online metric algorithms but does not address the deterministic $k$-server conjecture.
k-server/2111.10908.evidence: We present an $O((\log n)^2)$-competitive algorithm for metrical task systems (MTS) on any $n$-point metric space that is also $1$-competitive for service costs.
k-server/2111.10908.caveat: The paper focuses on metrical task systems (MTS) rather than the $k$-server problem, and its competitive ratio depends on the number of metric points $n$ rather than $k$.

k-server/2211.05753.claim: The authors disprove the randomized $k$-server conjecture by establishing an $\Omega(\log^2 k)$ lower bound on the randomized competitive ratio for the $k$-server problem.
k-server/2211.05753.evidence: There exist $(k+1)$-point metric spaces in which the randomized competitive ratio for the $k$-server problem is $\Omega(\log^2 k)$.
k-server/2211.05753.caveat: The paper refutes the randomized version of the conjecture rather than directly proving or disproving the deterministic $k$-competitiveness bound.

k-server/2302.05366.claim: The authors introduce a new framework for online algorithms with randomly infused advice and evaluate it on paging, uniform metrical task systems, and online set cover.
k-server/2302.05366.evidence: The applicability of the new RIA method is demonstrated by applying it to three extensively studied online problems: paging, uniform metrical task systems, and online set cover.
k-server/2302.05366.caveat: The paper investigates online algorithms within a model augmented by oracle advice rather than standard competitive analysis, and does not study the $k$-server problem on general metric spaces.

k-server/2403.11267.claim: The authors present results on reducing randomness in metrical task systems and collective metrical task systems, but do not address the deterministic $k$-server conjecture.
k-server/2403.11267.evidence: We consider metrical task systems on general metric spaces with $n$ points, and show that any fully randomized algorithm can be turned into a randomized algorithm that uses only $2\log n$ random bits, and achieves the same competitive ratio up to a factor $2$.
k-server/2403.11267.caveat: The abstract focuses on metrical task systems and randomized algorithms rather than the $k$-server problem and deterministic algorithms.

l-vs-p/2504.17412.claim: The authors derive improved catalytic space upper bounds for computing $SAC^2$ circuits and matrix powering, studying the catalytic space model rather than standard deterministic or nondeterministic logspace.
l-vs-p/2504.17412.evidence: Using register programs, we show that for every $ε> 0$, $SAC^2 \subseteq CSPACE\left(O\left(\frac{\log^2{n}}{\log\log{n}}\right), 2^{O(\log^{1+ε} n)}\right)$
l-vs-p/2504.17412.caveat: The work concerns catalytic space complexity $CSPACE$, an augmented space-bounded model with a reusable auxiliary tape, rather than standard logspace $\mathrm{L}$ or $\mathrm{NL}$.

l-vs-p/2506.16324.claim: The authors define and analyze quantum catalytic logspace, showing it can be simulated in quantum polynomial time, but they do not resolve the classical $\mathrm{L}$ vs $\mathrm{P}$ or $\mathrm{L}$ vs $\mathrm{NL}$ questions.
l-vs-p/2506.16324.evidence: First, we show that quantum catalytic logspace can always be computed quantumly in polynomial time; the classical analogue of this is the largest open question in catalytic computing.
l-vs-p/2506.16324.caveat: The paper investigates catalytic space complexity models rather than standard deterministic logarithmic space $\mathrm{L}$ or nondeterministic logarithmic space $\mathrm{NL}$.

l-vs-p/2510.12005.claim: The authors study in-place logspace complexity classes and catalytic space, showing that separating $\mathsf{inplaceFL}$ from $\mathsf{FL}$ would imply $\mathsf{SAT} \notin \mathsf{L}$ and demonstrating oracle barriers for proving $\mathsf{CL} \subseteq \mathsf{P}$.
l-vs-p/2510.12005.caveat: The results concern in-place multi-output function classes and catalytic space variants rather than directly resolving $\mathrm{L} = \mathrm{P}$ or $\mathrm{L} = \mathrm{NL}$.

l-vs-p/2604.24275.claim: The authors show that maximum matching in general graphs and several related algebraic/matroid problems can be solved in catalytic logspace ($\mathrm{CLP}$).
l-vs-p/2604.24275.evidence: In this paper, we show that we can construct $a \emph{maximum matching} in \emph{general graphs} in CL, and, in fact, in CLP$.
l-vs-p/2604.24275.caveat: The results are established in the catalytic logspace model ($\mathrm{CL}$ / $\mathrm{CLP}$), which grants the algorithm access to an arbitrary full catalytic memory, and thus does not directly yield inclusions or separations for standard deterministic logspace ($\mathrm{L}$) versus $\mathrm{P}$.

log-rank/1603.03757.claim: The authors prove an analogous log-rank conjecture proposed by Villagra et al. for nondeterministic multiparty quantum communication with message-passing, rather than the original Lovász–Saks log-rank conjecture.
log-rank/1603.03757.evidence: This characterisation allows us to prove a log-rank conjecture posed by Villagra et al. for nondeterministic multiparty quantum communication with message-passing.
log-rank/1603.03757.caveat: The result resolves a log-rank conjecture for a nondeterministic multiparty quantum model, not the classic two-party deterministic communication model of Lovász and Saks.

log-rank/1712.05735.claim: The authors prove the XOR Log-Rank Conjecture—a standard special case of the Log-Rank Conjecture for matrices of the form $M(x,y) = f(x \oplus y)$—for the restricted class of Boolean functions whose alternation is at most $\mathrm{poly}(\log n)$.
log-rank/1712.05735.evidence: As our main result, we show that, despite the above gap between $\al(f)$ $and \log \sp(f)$$, the XOR Log-Rank Conjecture is true for functions with the alternation upper bounded by $$poly(\log n)$$.
log-rank/1712.05735.caveat: The result applies only to the special case of XOR matrices $f(x \oplus y)$ rather than general Boolean matrices, and is further restricted to functions with alternation at most $\mathrm{poly}(\log n)$.

log-rank/1808.10191.claim: The authors rule out a potential proof strategy for the XOR log-rank conjecture (a special case of the log-rank conjecture) that relies on Huang's sensitivity theorem.
log-rank/1808.10191.evidence: Using this, we exhibit a family of Boolean functions that rule out a potential approach to settle the XOR Log-Rank conjecture via a proof of Sensitivity conjecture [Hao Huang (2019)].
log-rank/1808.10191.caveat: The result only rules out one specific proof route for the XOR variant of the conjecture and does not prove any new upper or lower bounds for the general log-rank conjecture.

log-rank/2101.09592.claim: The authors prove that the log-rank conjecture is equivalent to a conjecture in point-hyperplane incidence geometry and show that improving Lovett's bound on deterministic communication complexity would imply new bounds for bipartite subgraphs in incidence geometry.
log-rank/2101.09592.evidence: We prove that our conjecture is equivalent to the log-rank conjecture.
log-rank/2101.09592.caveat: The preprint does not prove the log-rank conjecture or improve the upper/lower bounds on deterministic communication complexity; it only establishes an equivalent geometric formulation and conditional implications.

log-rank/2312.09400.claim: The authors refute two published structural conjectures regarding the Fourier sparsity of Boolean functions that were proposed as candidate approaches to improve communication complexity bounds for XOR functions under the log-rank conjecture.
log-rank/2312.09400.evidence: In this note, we refute two conjectures.
log-rank/2312.09400.caveat: The paper refutes specific intermediate structural conjectures rather than establishing new bounds or resolving the log-rank conjecture itself.

log-rank/2401.00454.claim: The authors claim to prove the log-rank conjecture for all non-trivial total permutation-invariant Boolean functions.
log-rank/2401.00454.evidence: Furthermore, we show the Log-rank Conjecture holds for any non-trivial total permutation-invariant Boolean function.
log-rank/2401.00454.caveat: The result is restricted to the special case of total permutation-invariant Boolean functions rather than general Boolean matrices, and the preprint has not yet undergone peer review.

log-rank/2406.07859.claim: The authors establish structural relationships and equivalences among monotone complexity measures used in studying decision trees and special cases of communication complexity.
log-rank/2406.07859.evidence: In this article, we study the monotone analogues of standard measures like block sensitivity (mbs(f)), certificate complexity (MCC(f)) and fractional block sensitivity (fmbs(f)); and study the relationship between these measures given their connection with AND-decision tree and sparsity of a Boolean function.
log-rank/2406.07859.caveat: The paper focuses on Boolean function complexity measures rather than proving new bounds on deterministic communication complexity or the log-rank conjecture directly.

log-rank/2608.02533.claim: The author refutes the Alon-Saks-Seymour conjecture and proves an optimal communication lower bound for the Clique versus Independent Set problem, but does not claim to address the general log-rank conjecture.
log-rank/2608.02533.evidence: This leads to an optimal refutation of the Alon-Saks-Seymour conjecture, as well as an optimal communication lower bound for the Clique versus Independent Set problem, improving the previous results of Balodis, Ben-David, Göös, Jain and Kothari (FOCS 2021, SICOMP 2023) by several doubly logarithmic factors.

log-rank/2608.04141.claim: The preprint resolves a direct sum conjecture connecting zero-error information complexity to amortized randomized communication complexity, but it does not address the log-rank conjecture or deterministic communication complexity bounds in terms of matrix rank.
log-rank/2608.04141.evidence: In this paper, we resolve a central form of the direct sum conjecture in randomized communication complexity.

matrix-multiplication/2601.03020.claim: The authors do not make any claim about the value of $\omega$; instead, they use $\omega$ as an input parameter in conditional hardness lower bounds for regular expression matching.
matrix-multiplication/2601.03020.evidence: ...cannot be solved in time $n^{2-\varepsilon}\mathrm{tower}(o(\sqrt{m}))$ under OVC, $n^{\omega-\varepsilon}\mathrm{tower}(o(\sqrt{m}))$ under the $k$-Clique Hypothesis (where $\omega$ is the matrix multiplication exponent)...
matrix-multiplication/2601.03020.caveat: The preprint uses fast matrix multiplication algorithms and $\omega$ as a benchmark/parameter to prove conditional lower bounds for regex matching, without advancing the theoretical bounds on $\omega$ itself.

matrix-multiplication/2605.21738.claim: The authors present speedup theorems for asymptotic tensor rank, showing for example that the asymptotic rank of the small Coppersmith--Winograd tensor $\mathrm{cw}_2$ is less than $3.931$.
matrix-multiplication/2605.21738.evidence: For instance, we prove the asymptotic rank of $\mathrm{cw}_2$ is smaller than $3.931$, improving on $\underline{\mathrm{R}}(\mathrm{cw}_2)=4$.
matrix-multiplication/2605.21738.caveat: The result bounds the asymptotic rank of specific non-matrix multiplication tensors and does not yield a new upper bound on the matrix multiplication exponent $\omega$ itself.

matrix-multiplication/2608.16884.claim: The authors claim an improved upper bound on the matrix multiplication exponent of $\omega < 2.371177$.
matrix-multiplication/2608.16884.evidence: Our combined approach yields an upper bound of $ω$ < 2.371177, improving the previous best bound of 2.371339.
matrix-multiplication/2608.16884.caveat: The result is an incremental quantitative improvement on the upper bound obtained via AI-assisted optimization and does not prove $\omega = 2$.

matrix-multiplication/2608.24601.claim: The authors do not claim any new bounds or properties regarding $\omega$; rather, they use $\omega$ to state fine-grained conditional lower bounds for pushdown model checking.
matrix-multiplication/2608.24601.evidence: We prove that if the $3k$-Clique hypothesis (resp. combinatorial $3k$-Clique hypothesis) is true, then for any $ε> 0$, there is no algorithm (resp. combinatorial algorithm) that solves this problem in time $O((n^{(ω-1)k} |Σ| + n^{ωk})^{1-ε})$ (resp. $O((n^{2k} |Σ| + n^{3k})^{1-ε})$) where $ω$ is the matrix multiplication exponent.

nash-approximation/2604.27276.claim: The paper proves conditional PPAD-hardness results for approximate competitive equilibria in Fisher markets and explores the necessity of the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture, but it does not address $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibria in bimatrix games.
nash-approximation/2604.27276.evidence: We establish the first intractability result for the problem by showing that it is PPAD-hard for some constant $\delta> 0$, assuming the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture.
nash-approximation/2604.27276.caveat: The results apply to market equilibria in Fisher markets rather than Nash equilibria in two-player games.

nash-approximation/2607.10897.claim: The authors establish PPAD-hardness for computing approximate stationary Markov coarse correlated equilibria in two-player single-controller stochastic games.
nash-approximation/2607.10897.evidence: We resolve this question: computing an approximate stationary Markov CCE in two-player single-controller stochastic games is PPAD-complete, even with a fixed discount factor and binary actions.
nash-approximation/2607.10897.caveat: The paper addresses coarse correlated equilibria in stochastic Markov games rather than the polynomial-time approximation constant for Nash equilibria in static two-player bimatrix games.

nash-approximation/2608.30945.claim: The preprint provides a polynomial-time algorithm for the Győri-Lovász graph partitioning theorem and does not make any claims regarding approximating Nash equilibria in bimatrix games.
nash-approximation/2608.30945.evidence: No sentence in the abstract addresses approximating Nash equilibria in bimatrix games.

np-vs-conp/2302.06241.claim: The authors introduce and analyze the efficiency of proof systems based on hitting formulas (Hitting and Hitting(+)), establishing simulation relationships with tree-like resolution and Extended Frege, as well as an exponential lower bound for Hitting(+).
np-vs-conp/2302.06241.evidence: Using the ideas of PIT for noncommutative circuits [Raz-Shpilka,05] we show that Hitting is simulated by Extended Frege.
np-vs-conp/2302.06241.caveat: The exponential lower bound proved in the paper applies to a specific restricted system (Hitting(+)) rather than general proof systems like Frege or Extended Frege necessary to settle $\mathrm{NP}$ vs $\mathrm{coNP}$.

np-vs-conp/2405.02232.claim: The authors conditionally connect proof complexity lower bounds for the Implicit Extended Frege system ($%\mathsf{iEF}%$) to major circuit complexity separations such as $%\#\mathbf{P} \not\subseteq \mathbf{FP}/\operatorname{poly}%$.
np-vs-conp/2405.02232.evidence: In particular, we show that if $\mathsf{iEF}$ proves efficiently the standard derandomization assumption that a concrete Boolean function is hard on average for subexponential-size circuits, then any superpolynomial lower bound on the length of $\mathsf{iEF}$ proofs implies $\#\mathbf{P} \not\subseteq \mathbf{FP}/\operatorname{poly}$ (which would in turn imply, for example, $\mathbf{PSPACE} \not\subseteq \mathbf{P}/\operatorname{poly}$).
np-vs-conp/2405.02232.caveat: The paper proves a conditional implication between proof complexity lower bounds and circuit complexity separations, rather than establishing unconditional proof lower bounds or settling $\mathrm{NP} \neq \mathrm{coNP}$.

np-vs-conp/2606.27931.claim: The authors study relationships and polynomial equivalences between various propositional proof systems and TFNP search problems, but do not claim to settle whether $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{coNP}$ or prove lower bounds on Extended Frege.
np-vs-conp/2606.27931.evidence: We prove that <EF, Iter> is polynomially equivalent to the sequent calculus $G_1$, and also to the implicit Resolution proof system [EF, Resolution].
np-vs-conp/2606.27931.caveat: The abstract focuses on structural equivalences between proof systems and TFNP reductions rather than establishing superpolynomial lower bounds or resolving $\mathrm{NP} \neq \mathrm{coNP}$.

np-vs-conp/2608.08760.claim: The authors prove exponential proof size lower bounds for encodings of the weak rank principle in specific weak proof systems, namely $\mathrm{PCR}_{F_2}$ and Sherali--Adams.
np-vs-conp/2608.08760.evidence: We prove exponential size lower bounds for algebraic, perfect matching, and bamboo-tree encodings of WRank in PCR$_{F_2}$.
np-vs-conp/2608.08760.caveat: The lower bounds are proved for weak proof systems (Polynomial Calculus with Resolution over $\mathbb{F}_2$ and Sherali--Adams) rather than strong systems like Frege or Extended Frege, and thus do not settle whether $\mathrm{NP} = \mathrm{coNP}$.

p-vs-bpp/2411.06569.claim: The authors construct an efficient randomized black-box polynomial identity testing algorithm for constant-depth $+$-regular non-commutative circuits.
p-vs-bpp/2411.06569.evidence: We present a randomized black-box polynomial-time algorithm for +-regular circuits of any constant depth.
p-vs-bpp/2411.06569.caveat: The algorithm is randomized rather than deterministic and applies only to a restricted class of non-commutative circuits, so it does not contribute to the derandomization of PIT or $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{BPP}$.

p-vs-bpp/2507.22265.claim: The authors present a derandomization of semi-random $k$-XOR refutation analysis with applications to cell-probe lower bounds and range avoidance for $\mathsf{NC}^0$ circuits, rather than addressing general derandomization ($\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}$).
p-vs-bpp/2507.22265.evidence: Our result can be viewed as a complete derandomization of the state-of-the-art semi-random $k$-XOR refutation analysis (Guruswami, Kothari and Manohar, STOC 2022, Hsieh, Kothari and Mohanty, SODA 2023), which complements the derandomization of the even-arity case obtained by Korten et al.
p-vs-bpp/2507.22265.caveat: The work focuses on specific computational problems (cell-probe lower bounds, CSP refutation, and range avoidance for $\mathsf{NC}^0$) rather than proving $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}$.

p-vs-bpp/2509.11349.claim: The authors construct efficient randomized and deterministic polynomial-time identity testing algorithms for polynomials over nonassociative algebras.
p-vs-bpp/2509.11349.evidence: On the derandomization side, we give a deterministic polynomial-time identity testing algorithm for nonassociative polynomials given by arithmetic circuits in the white-box setting.
p-vs-bpp/2509.11349.caveat: The results are restricted to the nonassociative polynomial setting and do not apply to general standard arithmetic circuits or arbitrary $\mathrm{BPP}$ languages.

p-vs-bpp/2602.09302.claim: The authors introduce a new bounded arithmetic theory, $APX_1$, to study the proof-theoretic strength and provability of derandomization statements such as $\mathrm{prBPP} = \mathrm{prP}$ within deterministic feasible mathematics.
p-vs-bpp/2602.09302.evidence: In particular, the framework we develop for $APX_1$ enables the formulation of precise questions concerning the provability of prBPP=prP in deterministic feasible mathematics.
p-vs-bpp/2602.09302.caveat: The paper addresses the formal provability of derandomization conjectures in bounded arithmetic rather than proving or disproving whether $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{BPP}$ holds unconditionally.

p-vs-bpp/2602.10030.claim: The authors construct optimal pseudorandom generators for degree-$d$ polynomials over fields of size $q \approx d^4$ assuming sufficiently large characteristic.
p-vs-bpp/2602.10030.evidence: In this work, we construct the first PRG with optimal seed length for degree-$d$ polynomials over fields of polynomial size, specifically $q \approx d^4$, assuming sufficiently large characteristic.
p-vs-bpp/2602.10030.caveat: The PRG construction is limited to the specific algebraic model of low-degree polynomials over polynomial-size fields with large characteristic, rather than derandomizing general $\mathrm{BPP}$ computations.

p-vs-bpp/2602.13449.claim: The authors present a deterministic quasi-polynomial-time black-box polynomial identity testing algorithm for the restricted model of read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs.
p-vs-bpp/2602.13449.evidence: Thus, we obtain the first order-oblivious deterministic black-box PIT algorithm for ROABPs, running in quasi-polynomial time $n\cdot(wd)^{O(w^2)}$.
p-vs-bpp/2602.13449.caveat: The algorithm applies only to the specific restricted model of read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs (ROABPs) rather than general polynomial identity testing or general BPP algorithms.

p-vs-bpp/2603.25095.claim: The authors present derandomization techniques for edge sampling in graphs using bounded independence, showing that specific randomized graph algorithms can be explicitly derandomized.
p-vs-bpp/2603.25095.evidence: We show that the optimal algorithms of Khanna, Putterman, and Song (arxiv 2025) can be explicitly derandomized while maintaining near-optimality.
p-vs-bpp/2603.25095.caveat: The paper focuses on derandomizing specific edge-subsampling techniques and parallel graph algorithms rather than addressing general randomized computation ($\\mathrm{BPP}$) or polynomial identity testing.

p-vs-bpp/2603.27398.claim: The author claims to prove that the Shortest Vector Problem is $\mathbf{NP}$-hard under deterministic reductions by derandomizing Ajtai's randomized reduction, but this does not settle general derandomization or whether $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}$.
p-vs-bpp/2603.27398.evidence: In this paper, we prove this conjecture, thereby derandomizing Ajtai's classical randomized hardness result (1998).
p-vs-bpp/2603.27398.caveat: The derandomization is specific to a reduction for the Shortest Vector Problem in lattices rather than general randomized complexity classes or polynomial-time algorithms.

p-vs-bpp/2604.17061.claim: The authors relate the deterministic complexity of hyperdeterminant vanishing to structured instances of polynomial identity testing, without resolving $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{BPP}$ generally.
p-vs-bpp/2604.17061.evidence: We show that deterministic hardness transfer to the hyperdeterminant reduces to selecting a point outside the zero set of a completion polynomial, yielding a structured instance of polynomial identity testing.
p-vs-bpp/2604.17061.caveat: The paper focuses on tensor degeneracy and hyperdeterminant complexity, using polynomial identity testing as a framework rather than providing a deterministic algorithm for general PIT or proving $\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{BPP}$.

p-vs-nc/2606.24845.claim: The authors present an $O(n^{1/3}\text{log}^{1/3}n)$-round parallel algorithm for computing a matroid basis, matching the established oracle lower bound.
p-vs-nc/2606.24845.evidence: Our algorithm runs in $O(n^{1/3}\log^{1/3}n)$ rounds, matching the lower bound of KUW up to a $\text{log}^{2/3}(n)$ factor.
p-vs-nc/2606.24845.caveat: The result addresses parallel round complexity in the independence oracle model for matroid basis computation rather than general circuit complexity bounds for $\mathrm{P}$ vs $\mathrm{NC}$.

p-vs-nc/2607.24668.claim: The preprint proves the NP-completeness and #P-completeness of certain independent set variants on polyominoes, but does not address the relationship between $\mathrm{P}$ and $\mathrm{NC}$ or parallel circuit complexity.
p-vs-nc/2607.24668.evidence: We prove that INDQUEENS on polyominoes is NP-complete, proving a conjecture of Langlois-Rémillard--Müßig--Roldán.

p-vs-nc/2608.29902.claim: The paper does not make any claims regarding the $\mathrm{P}$ vs $\mathrm{NC}$ problem.
p-vs-nc/2608.29902.evidence: No sentence in the abstract addresses the $\mathrm{P}$ vs $\mathrm{NC}$ problem or circuit complexity.

p-vs-np/2512.11820.claim: The author claims to establish that $\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}$ within $\mathrm{ZFC}$ using an algebraic separation framework based on sum-of-squares polynomials and SPDP rank bounds.
p-vs-np/2512.11820.evidence: Together these yield a contradiction under the assumption P = NP, establishing a separation.
p-vs-np/2512.11820.caveat: The proof relies on complex, novel mathematical machinery (such as SPDP rank and contextual entanglement width) and has not undergone peer review or machine-checked formal verification to ensure there are no subtle gaps or hidden invalid assumptions.

p-vs-np/2602.09302.claim: The authors introduce a bounded arithmetic theory $APX_1$ to study the provability of complexity-theoretic statements, citing the provability of $\mathrm{P}$ versus $\mathrm{NP}$ in bounded arithmetic as motivation without claiming to solve or directly advance $\mathrm{P}$ versus $\mathrm{NP}$.
p-vs-np/2602.09302.evidence: Since the (un)provability of P versus NP in bounded arithmetic has long served as a central theme in the field, we expect this line of investigation to be of particular interest.

planted-clique/2402.05451.claim: The authors prove tight query-complexity phase transitions for non-adaptive low-degree algorithms detecting a planted clique in sublinear time in the regime $k = \Theta(n^{1/2 + \delta})$ for $\delta > 0$.
planted-clique/2402.05451.evidence: We prove a computational phase transition for this class of non-adaptive low-degree algorithms: under the scaling $\lvert M \rvert = \Theta(n^\gamma)$, the clique can be detected when $\gamma > 3(1/2 - \delta) but not when \gamma < 3(1/2 - \delta)$.
planted-clique/2402.05451.caveat: The preprint studies query complexity and sublinear-time trade-offs for planted cliques of size $k > \sqrt{n}$ ($k = \Theta(n^{1/2+\delta})$) rather than addressing the open question of detecting cliques of size $k < \sqrt{n}$ in polynomial time.

planted-clique/2404.14159.claim: The authors give a fast $O(n^{2.872})$-time greedy algorithm for list-decoding planted cliques in a semirandom model when $k \ge O(\sqrt{n} \log^2 n)$.
planted-clique/2404.14159.evidence: We give a simple, greedy $O(n^{\omega+0.5})=O(n^{2.872})$-time algorithm to list-decode planted cliques in a semirandom model introduced in [CSV17] (following [FK01]) that succeeds whenever the size of the planted clique is $k\geq O(\sqrt{n} \log^2 n)$.
planted-clique/2404.14159.caveat: The algorithm works in a semirandom model and requires $k \ge O(\sqrt{n} \log^2 n)$, so it does not break the $\sqrt{n}$ algorithmic barrier for standard planted clique.

polynomial-hirsch/1611.08039.claim: The authors study structural equivalences and conjectures for the circuit diameter, a relaxation/variant of the combinatorial diameter where walks follow circuit directions rather than edges of the 1-skeleton.
polynomial-hirsch/1611.08039.evidence: We consider analogous properties for a variant of the combinatorial diameter called the circuit diameter.
polynomial-hirsch/1611.08039.caveat: The results pertain to circuit diameter rather than the standard combinatorial diameter of polytopes.

polynomial-hirsch/2302.03977.claim: The authors study whether known counterexamples to variants of the Hirsch conjecture transfer to the circuit setting, showing that Santos' bounded counterexamples do not provide counterexamples for the circuit diameter conjecture.
polynomial-hirsch/2302.03977.evidence: Our main contribution is to show that the original counterexamples for the other variants, for bounded polytopes and using monotone walks, also do not transfer.
polynomial-hirsch/2302.03977.caveat: The paper focuses on the circuit diameter setting and specific known counterexamples rather than proving general upper or lower bounds on combinatorial diameter.

polynomial-hirsch/2602.06958.claim: The authors establish a strongly polynomial upper bound on the circuit diameter of polyhedra, which is a relaxation of the combinatorial diameter.
polynomial-hirsch/2602.06958.evidence: We prove a strongly polynomial bound on the circuit diameter of polyhedra, resolving the circuit analogue of the polynomial Hirsch conjecture.
polynomial-hirsch/2602.06958.caveat: The result bounds the circuit diameter rather than the combinatorial diameter; because circuit steps relax edge steps, an upper bound on circuit diameter does not imply a polynomial upper bound on the combinatorial diameter.

seth/2507.13337.claim: The authors introduce a benchmark dataset for testing AI models on algorithmic reasoning problems, mentioning that some benchmark tasks are related to central complexity conjectures like the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), without claiming to resolve SETH.
seth/2507.13337.evidence: Third, many of our problems are intimately related to the frontier of theoretical computer science, and to central conjectures therein, such as the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH).
seth/2507.13337.caveat: The paper focuses on evaluating AI reasoning performance via a benchmark dataset rather than presenting theoretical algorithms or complexity proofs regarding SETH.

seth/2509.14489.claim: The authors do not claim to resolve or make progress on SETH, but instead use SETH as a conditional assumption to prove lower bounds for depth-2 linear circuits.
seth/2509.14489.evidence: The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis implies an $N^{1 + \Omega(1)}$ size lower bound for depth-2 linear circuits computing the Walsh--Hadamard transform (and the disjointness matrix with a technical caveat), and proving a $N^{1 + \Omega(1)}$ depth-2 size lower bound would also imply breakthrough threshold circuit lower bounds.

seth/2510.12232.claim: The authors do not claim to resolve or progress SETH, but rather cite SETH-based lower bounds as motivation for studying practical algorithms for the Dominating $H$-Pattern problem.
seth/2510.12232.evidence: Fine-grained complexity results show that on worst-case inputs, any significant improvement over the naive brute-force algorithm is unlikely, as this would refute the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis.
seth/2510.12232.caveat: The paper is an algorithm engineering work focusing on practical implementations and heuristic search pruning rather than proving theoretical algorithm bounds for SAT or SETH.

seth/2602.05186.claim: The authors do not attempt to solve SETH, but instead assume its truth to show that the Gap-sensitive Co-Linear Chaining problem cannot be solved in sub-quadratic time.
seth/2602.05186.evidence: We show that solving the Gap-CLC problem in sub-quadratic time is highly unlikely unless the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis fails -- even when restricted to binary alphabets.
seth/2602.05186.caveat: The paper uses SETH as a hypothesis to prove lower bounds for sequence-to-graph alignment rather than addressing the truth of SETH itself.

seth/2603.12999.claim: The authors assume SETH (and ETH) to establish tight conditional lower bounds for Bin Packing and several multi-machine scheduling problems, rather than proving or disproving SETH itself.
seth/2603.12999.evidence: We prove tight lower bounds based on the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) for several classic $k$-machine scheduling problems, including makespan minimisation with release dates ($P_k|r_j|C_{\max}$), minimizing the number of tardy jobs ($P_k||ΣU_j$), and minimizing the weighted sum of completion times ($P_k || Σw_j C_j$).
seth/2603.12999.caveat: The paper uses SETH as an unproven conditional hypothesis to show algorithm hardness for other problems, rather than making progress on the truth value of SETH itself.

seth/2605.04798.claim: The authors do not attempt to prove or disprove the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, but instead use a non-uniform variant of SETH as a conditional hardness assumption to prove lower bounds for data structure problems.
seth/2605.04798.evidence: Under the Non-Uniform Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, we also prove arbitrarily large polynomial space lower bounds for any $\mathsf{OnlineOV}$ data structure with sublinear query time even with computationally unbounded preprocessing.
seth/2605.04798.caveat: The paper assumes SETH as a hypothesis to deduce lower bounds for other problems, rather than proving or refuting SETH itself.

seth/2606.25887.claim: The authors do not address the truth of SETH itself, but rather assume SETH as a hypothesis to prove conditional quadratic lower bounds for computational geometry problems in superconstant dimension.
seth/2606.25887.evidence: Chen [Theory Comput. 2020] proved that, assuming the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), these problems require $n^{2-o(1)}$ time when the dimension satisfies $d=2^{Θ(\text{log}^* n)}$.
seth/2606.25887.caveat: The paper assumes SETH to derive conditional lower bounds for geometric problems rather than attempting to prove or disprove SETH.

seth/2607.05040.claim: The authors study the fine-grained complexity of counting hypergraph motifs based on the Triangle Hypothesis and Hyperclique Hypothesis, without making any claims about the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH) or CNF-SAT.
seth/2607.05040.evidence: For all non-degenerate Venn diagrams, we show that no FPT-near-linear-time algorithm exists unless either the Triangle Hypothesis or the Hyperclique Hypothesis fails.
seth/2607.05040.caveat: The paper focuses on fine-grained lower bounds for hypergraph motif counting assuming the Triangle and Hyperclique Hypotheses, and does not directly address SETH or algorithms for $k$-SAT.

seth/2608.24601.claim: The preprint does not address the Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis (SETH), but rather establishes conditional lower bounds for pushdown model checking assuming the $3k$-Clique hypothesis.
seth/2608.24601.evidence: We prove that if the $3k$-Clique hypothesis (resp. combinatorial $3k$-Clique hypothesis) is true, then for any $ε> 0$, there is no algorithm (resp. combinatorial algorithm) that solves this problem in time $O((n^{(ω-1)k} |Σ| + n^{ωk})^{1-ε})$ (resp. $O((n^{2k} |Σ| + n^{3k})^{1-ε})$) where $ω$ is the matrix multiplication exponent.
seth/2608.24601.caveat: The abstract does not mention SETH or CNF-SAT algorithms, focusing instead on fine-grained lower bounds derived from $3k$-Clique.

strongly-polynomial-lp/2608.13983.claim: The authors do not address general linear programming, but present strongly polynomial-time algorithms for specific matroid partitioning and fair allocation problems.
strongly-polynomial-lp/2608.13983.evidence: As applications, we obtain an additive guarantee for matroid-constrained makespan minimization for identical machines and a strongly polynomial-time algorithm for finding an EF1 allocation under a matroid constraint and identical additive valuations.
strongly-polynomial-lp/2608.13983.caveat: The strongly polynomial algorithms in this paper apply to specific combinatorial and matroid-constrained problems rather than general linear programs.

sunflower/1801.09488.claim: The authors do not claim to advance or resolve the sunflower conjecture itself, but rather use it as a conditional hypothesis to yield faster algorithms for certain SAT problems.
sunflower/1801.09488.evidence: Furthermore, if the sunflower conjecture holds for sunflowers with k sets, then the partial k-NU language has an improved algorithm via local search.
sunflower/1801.09488.caveat: The paper assumes the sunflower conjecture to prove algorithmic results rather than proving any new bounds on the conjecture itself.

sunflower/2010.04985.claim: The authors do not claim to advance the sunflower conjecture itself, but rather utilize relaxed sunflower lemmas as a technique to prove structural theorems for local algorithms.
sunflower/2010.04985.evidence: Our techniques strongly rely on relaxed sunflower lemmas and the Hajnal-Szemerédi theorem.
sunflower/2010.04985.caveat: The paper applies existing or variant sunflower lemmas as a tool to tackle problems in property testing and coding theory, rather than attempting to prove new bounds for the Erdős–Rado sunflower conjecture.

sunflower/2209.03326.claim: The authors do not claim any progress on the sunflower conjecture itself, but instead apply the set-theoretic spread property developed in recent sunflower breakthroughs to a variant of the second Kahn--Kalai conjecture.
sunflower/2209.03326.evidence: The bound follows by a direct application of the set-theoretic "spread" property, which led to recent breakthroughs in the sunflower conjecture by Alweiss, Lovett, Wu and Zhang and the first fractional Kahn--Kalai conjecture by Frankston, Kahn, Narayanan and Park.

tsp-subtour-gap/2507.07003.claim: The authors claim that the integrality gap of the subtour elimination relaxation for metric TSP is $4/3$ for instances where the optimal LP solution has at most $n+6$ non-zero components.
tsp-subtour-gap/2507.07003.evidence: We prove that, when solving a problem on n nodes, if the optimal SEP solution has at most n + 6 non-zero components, then the conjecture is true.
tsp-subtour-gap/2507.07003.caveat: The result is restricted to LP solutions with sparse support (at most $n+6$ non-zero entries) rather than arbitrary metric TSP instances, and relies in part on computational verification.

tsp-subtour-gap/2604.05645.claim: The preprint presents improved space-time tradeoffs for exact algorithms for general TSP, which does not address the integrality gap of the Held–Karp LP relaxation for metric TSP.
tsp-subtour-gap/2604.05645.evidence: In this paper we give a tradeoff that strictly improves all previous ones for all $2 < T < 4$, achieving a minimum of $ST < 3.572$.

tsp-subtour-gap/2606.31907.claim: The authors present improved bicriteria approximation algorithms for bounded-degree and subset variants of the Traveling Salesman Problem rather than addressing the integrality gap of the subtour LP for general metric TSP.
tsp-subtour-gap/2606.31907.evidence: We present improved algorithms for several bounded-degree traveling salesman problems.
tsp-subtour-gap/2606.31907.caveat: The paper studies TSP with degree constraints and subset TSP variants, providing bicriteria approximations rather than bounding the integrality gap of the Held--Karp relaxation for standard metric TSP.

union-closed/2004.05210.claim: The authors study a linear relaxation of an integer programming formulation of Frankl's conjecture and prove an upper bound of $f(n,a) = O(a^2)$, whereas establishing $f(n,a) \le 2a$ would prove the conjecture.
union-closed/2004.05210.evidence: By considering the linear relaxation of the integer programming formulation that was proposed in New Conjectures for Union-Closed Families by Pulaj, Raymond and Theis, we prove that $O(a^2)$ is an upper bound for $f(n,a)$.
union-closed/2004.05210.caveat: The bound $f(n,a) = O(a^2)$ derived from the linear programming relaxation is substantially weaker than the $f(n,a) \le 2a$ bound required to resolve the union-closed sets conjecture.

union-closed/2408.11213.claim: The authors introduce structural reduction techniques for union-closed families and prove Frankl's conjecture for a specific subclass of families constructed from power sets via these reductions.
union-closed/2408.11213.evidence: Finally, we show that Frankl's Conjecture holds for the class of families obtained from successively applying the reduction process to a power set.
union-closed/2408.11213.caveat: The proof of Frankl's conjecture is restricted to a specific family generated by the authors' reduction process rather than the general conjecture.

union-closed/2607.07564.claim: The preprint proves a different conjecture of Frankl concerning the binomial norm of intersecting-union families, and does not address the union-closed sets conjecture.
union-closed/2607.07564.evidence: In this paper, we prove Frankl's conjecture and determine all extremal families.
union-closed/2607.07564.caveat: The conjecture proved in this paper concerns binomial norm bounds $\lVert\mathcal F\rVert_n \le \frac{n+1}{6}$ for intersecting-union families, which is entirely distinct from Frankl's union-closed sets conjecture.

unique-games/2304.07612.claim: The author proves a spectral characterization of small set expansion via $p$-to-$q$ hypercontractivity of top eigenspaces, advancing tools closely linked to the study of the Small Set Expansion Hypothesis and Unique Games.
unique-games/2304.07612.evidence: We prove a generalization of Cheeger's inequality, giving an algebraic condition equivalent to small set expansion.
unique-games/2304.07612.caveat: The paper proves a structural graph-theoretic result about small set expansion rather than directly addressing the computational hardness of Unique Games or settling the Unique Games Conjecture.

unique-games/2506.12021.claim: The authors do not claim to resolve or make progress on the Unique Games Conjecture, but instead use it as an assumption to derive conditional inapproximability bounds for the Monitoring Edge-Geodetic Set problem.
unique-games/2506.12021.evidence: Furthermore, we present inapproximability results, proving that the MEG-set optimization problem is $\mathcal{APX}$-Hard and that, if the unique games conjecture holds, the problem is not approximable within a factor of $2-\epsilon$ for any constant $\epsilon> 0$.

unique-games/2511.20338.claim: The authors establish that maintaining bipartite colourings on temporal graphs is NP-hard to approximate within any constant factor assuming the Unique Games Conjecture holds.
unique-games/2511.20338.evidence: On the negative side, we show that, despite bipartite colouring being easy on static graphs, the problem of maintaining such a colouring on graphs that are bipartite in each snapshot is NP-Hard to even approximate within $\emph{any} constant factor unless the Unique Games Conjecture fails$.
unique-games/2511.20338.caveat: The paper uses the Unique Games Conjecture as an assumption to prove conditional inapproximability for a temporal graph problem, rather than proving or making progress toward the conjecture itself.

unique-games/2602.10368.claim: The authors assume the Unique Games Conjecture to prove conditional hardness results and optimal trade-offs for robust satisfiability of promise constraint satisfaction problems.
unique-games/2602.10368.evidence: For the PCSP 1-in-3-SAT vs NAE-SAT with negations, we prove that it is hard, under the Unique Games conjecture (UGC), to satisfy $1-\Omega(1/\log (1/\epsilon))$ constraints in a $(1-\epsilon)$-satisfiable instance.
unique-games/2602.10368.caveat: The paper uses the Unique Games Conjecture as a conditional hypothesis rather than making progress towards proving or disproving the conjecture itself.

unique-games/2605.09815.claim: The paper does not solve or advance the Unique Games Conjecture itself, but rather uses a related hypothesis—the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture—as a conditional assumption to establish a complexity dichotomy for a class of Promise MMSNP problems.
unique-games/2605.09815.evidence: For this class, we obtain a full complexity classification conditional on the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture, a recently proposed perfect-completeness surrogate of the Unique Games Conjecture.
unique-games/2605.09815.caveat: The authors assume the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture as a hypothesis to derive hardness results in promise constraint satisfaction problems, rather than proving any new result about the Unique Games Conjecture.

unique-games/2605.27098.claim: The author uses the Unique Games Conjecture as an assumption to establish improved NP-hardness of approximation results for social choice and allocation problems, rather than making progress on proving or disproving the conjecture itself.
unique-games/2605.27098.evidence: We use this test to prove the following hardness results (assuming the unique games conjecture is true): (1) We show that it is NP-hard to approximate the max Nash welfare by a factor better than $\sqrt[3]{\frac{81}{65}} - \varepsilon \approx 1.0761$.
unique-games/2605.27098.caveat: The paper assumes the truth of the Unique Games Conjecture rather than proving it.

unique-games/2608.00333.claim: The preprint assumes the Unique Games Conjecture to establish conditional NP-hardness of approximation results for MAX-3-CUT and Quantum MAX-CUT, rather than making progress on proving or refuting the conjecture itself.
unique-games/2608.00333.evidence: Assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, we show it is NP-hard to approximate MAX-3-CUT within a multiplicative factor of $α_3+ε$ for every $ε>0$, where $α_3\frac{}{} \text{is...}$
unique-games/2608.00333.caveat: The paper relies on the Unique Games Conjecture as an unproven hypothesis rather than attempting to prove or refute it.

unique-games/2608.04883.claim: The authors assume the Unique Games Conjecture to establish that Cluster Deletion is $\mathrm{NP}$-hard to approximate within a factor of $2-\epsilon$ for any fixed $\epsilon > 0$.
unique-games/2608.04883.evidence: We rule out this possibility under the Unique Games Conjecture: Cluster Deletion is NP-hard to approximate within a factor of $2-\epsilon$ for every fixed $\epsilon>0$, matching the known $2$-approximation [Veldt et al., WWW 2018].
unique-games/2608.04883.caveat: The paper assumes the Unique Games Conjecture as a hardness hypothesis rather than making progress toward proving or disproving the conjecture itself.

unique-games/2608.05331.claim: The preprint does not claim to advance or resolve the Unique Games Conjecture itself, but instead provides an improved approximation algorithm for Boolean Max-$k$-CSP whose limits are compared against known UGC-conditional hardness bounds.
unique-games/2608.05331.evidence: Assuming the Unique Games Conjecture, De and Mossel (arXiv:1202.5258) showed that achieving an approximation ratio better than $(k+1)/2^k$ for odd $k$ and $(k+2)/2^k$ for even $k$, is NP-hard.
unique-games/2608.05331.caveat: The paper uses the Unique Games Conjecture only as a benchmark for NP-hardness bounds rather than investigating the conjecture directly.

unit-distances/2606.25887.claim: The authors do not claim a new bound on the Erdős unit distance problem, but instead prove fine-grained complexity lower bounds for the Furthest Pair problem under SETH.
unit-distances/2606.25887.evidence: The proof utilizes techniques in OpenAI's recent disproof of the Erdos unit distance conjecture.
unit-distances/2606.25887.caveat: The paper addresses computational complexity lower bounds for geometric algorithms under SETH rather than bounds on the maximum number of unit distances.

unit-distances/2607.05374.claim: The authors claim to construct a point set in the plane with $n^{1+\delta}$ occurrences of a single distance for some constant $\delta > 0$, thereby disproving Erdős's unit distance conjecture.
unit-distances/2607.05374.evidence: Taking $A=P$, the inequality above gives a distance occurring $n^{1+δ}$ times in $P$; thereby a scaled copy of $P$ is a counterexample for the unit-distance conjecture.
unit-distances/2607.05374.caveat: The preprint has not yet undergone peer review to verify the validity of its construction and proof.

unit-distances/2608.28997.claim: The authors do not claim any mathematical result on the Erdős unit distance problem, referencing it only as a contextual example in a study on formal proof verification.
unit-distances/2608.28997.evidence: No sentence in the abstract supports a mathematical claim regarding the Erdős unit distance problem.
unit-distances/2608.28997.caveat: The paper is a meta-analysis of machine-checked proof systems rather than a technical contribution to discrete geometry.
